title: Why an Amphitheater Would Not Work in La Azteca: The Flood Risk Is Zacate Creek
excerpt: A community idea to put an outdoor amphitheater in La Azteca runs into the neighborhood's flood record: the Zacate Creek corridor carries Laredo's greatest flood exposure, and the creek has hit near-record levels in three of the last four years.
content:
A community proposal circulating this week would turn a space in La Azteca into an outdoor amphitheater for movie nights, live music, cultural festivals and local vendors. The aspiration is easy to understand. La Azteca is one of Laredo's oldest neighborhoods, rich in history and culture, and it deserves investment. The problem is the site. An amphitheater built in the wrong part of La Azteca would sit in the path of the water, and the record shows the water comes back.

La Azteca's flood risk is Zacate Creek. The neighborhood's residential core sits on a high bluff above the Rio Grande, but its eastern edge is the Zacate Creek corridor, a greenbelt along the creek. The bluff is safe ground. The corridor is not, and any amphitheater would be built in the corridor, not on the bluff.

About 15,000 Laredo residents, 5.7 percent of the city, live in the Federal Emergency Management Agency's high-risk flood zone, the 1 percent annual chance zone also called the 100-year floodplain. About 6,200 of them, 42 percent of everyone in that zone, live along Zacate Creek alone, more than along any other waterway in the city. Chacon Creek follows with about 3,400, and Las Manadas Creek with about 1,800. The FEMA flood map panels in force for nearly every Laredo resident took effect in 2008.

The history is written in the same place. On June 29, 1954, floodwaters from Hurricane Alice pushed the Rio Grande to a crest of nearly 62 feet, the second-largest flood in Laredo's recorded history. The largest was in 1865. In 1954, the water did not reach the front doors of homes on the higher, elevated ground of the Azteca neighborhood. The people living lower down, near Zacate Creek, were not so fortunate. Dr. Jerry Thompson, a historian at Texas A&M International University and author of 'Laredo: A Pictorial History,' put it plainly: 'A lot of people were displaced, especially those living along Zacate Creek.'

The risk is not history alone. The U.S. Geological Survey gauge on Zacate Creek at Laredo recorded 8.5 feet on September 15, 2023, the highest in its record going back to 2015. It recorded 8.4 feet on September 25, 2025, and 8.0 feet on May 28, 2024. In a normal year the creek tops out around 7.5 feet. Near-record water has come in three of the last four years. And in July 2026, the City of Laredo issued an official update on Rio Grande flooding, with the river near 20 feet and parks along the river affected. The river system floods in the present, not only in the history books.

That is why a tiered outdoor bowl is the wrong structure for this ground. A bowl collects standing water. A permanent amphitheater in the corridor would face repeated inundation and silt and debris damage, floodplain development permitting, flood insurance costs, and a life-safety problem no design fully resolves. Zacate Creek is a flashy urban waterway that rises fast, and a crowd seated in a bowl is the wrong place for a rapid rise.

Laredo does not need to build a second amphitheater. It already has one, in the same corridor. The City of Laredo's Zacate Creek Green District Corridor project is developing 22 acres along the creek with $7.6 million in local, state and federal funds, including a $3,799,966 federal Outdoor Recreation Legacy Partnership grant announced March 27, 2024. The project includes restoration of the existing amphitheater, embankment stabilization, trails, a visitor center, and kayak and bicycle rental. The city issued a request for qualifications for the renovation design on September 13, 2026, with responses due November 19, 2026. The amphitheater programming belongs there, in a venue designed for the floodplain, with flood-aware scheduling.

The downtown stage already exists too. San Agustin Plaza, at 1012 Grant Street, already hosts the programming an amphitheater would bring: the Jamboozie music festival and the Laredo Cultural District's free 'Music in the Plaza' concert series, most recently a free concert on October 16, 2026. And for large audiences, the Lake Casa Blanca International State Park amphitheater on U.S. Highway 59 is an active venue.

One caution belongs in this account. The community proposal does not identify a specific parcel, so no parcel-level FEMA determination exists for the proposed lot. This analysis is at the neighborhood and corridor level, and any specific lot would need its own FEMA check before a final judgment. But the corridor-level record is clear enough to say this: the idea deserves a home, and the home is not the floodplain. Saying no to the site is not saying no to the neighborhood. La Azteca's revitalization is already underway through the creek greenbelt investment, and that is where the amphitheater already stands.

Sources: U.S. Geological Survey; National Park Service and U.S. Department of the Interior; BestNeighborhood analysis of FEMA flood data; City of Laredo; Dr. Jerry Thompson, Texas A&M International University; Texas Parks and Wildlife Department.
